 We found no regulator warning that names a sender called Education Connection, so we cannot call the name itself a scam. We can tell you how student loan and school scams work, how to judge any message that uses an education sounding name, and what to do if you already replied or paid.
 By Ugnius Kiguolis Published November 1, 2026 10 min read 
 Facts checked November 1, 2026. Removal steps tested on Windows 11 (26H2) and checked against Microsoft's and the browser makers' current documentation.
 Do it yourself · free Remove Education Connection scam yourself 4 steps, about 12 minutes, no software needed. 
 Start the steps ↓ The usual shape of a student loan or school scam, from the FTC's and the Education Department's descriptions. It is a general pattern, not a finding about one named sender. Education Connection scam: summary
 Name Education Connection scam (a search phrase, not a confirmed sender) 
 Type Possible scam text, call or email built around education, student loans or school enrolment; the name is also a vague label that could be used by genuine and fake senders 
 Risk Depends on the message: low if it only offers information, high if it asks for a fee, a login, an ID number or a card number 
 Symptoms An unexpected text, call or email about loan forgiveness, a grant, a refund, unpaid tuition or school enrolment, often with a deadline 
 How to get rid of it Nothing to uninstall. Do not click or reply, check the claim with your school or loan servicer yourself, report the message, and change passwords if you gave a login 
 Our check (1 November 2026) Desk check only: no site, sender number or message was tested, and no URLhaus entry exists for this name 
 Show 6 more facts Search demand About 110 people a month search for this phrase with a security question 
 Devices Phones, computers and landlines: it arrives as a text, a call or an email 
 Microsoft detection None. This is a message and a pretext, not a program 
 Evidence 0 reports from affected users; details still limited 
 First seen 1 November 2026 
 Facts checked 1 November 2026 
 Desk check of 1 November 2026: we read the FTC's page on student loan and education scams and searched for official warnings and enforcement cases. We made no request to any address and saw no message sent under this name.
 Several points come from search summaries of the Education Department inspector general's fraud alert, a District of Columbia regulator notice and press reports of two FTC cases, and are marked as such in the text.
 Is Education Connection a scam?
 We cannot say that a sender called Education Connection is a scam, and we cannot say it is safe. We searched for a warning from a regulator, a school or a security company that names it and found none. What we did find is a well documented kind of fraud that uses education sounding names, so the safe answer is to judge each message by what it asks of you.
 The phrase is searched by about 110 people a month with a security question, which tells us that real people are receiving something under this name and doubting it. It does not tell us what the something is.
 A text, a phone call, an email, a website form and a mailed letter can all carry such a name, and the name is generic enough that several unrelated senders could use it. Some of them may be genuine businesses, such as a school, a training provider or a company that connects students with schools. Others may be fraudsters who picked a name that sounds official.
 We are not allowed to name a real business as a scam without a primary source, and we have none. So this page does not accuse anyone.
 It tells you what is and is not confirmed, gives you a short test you can run on any message in two minutes, and lists the steps if you have already answered. If your message passes none of the tests below, treat it as a scam whatever the sender calls itself.
 What the name is A generic education sounding label seen as a search phrase; no confirmed owner Confirmed Student loan and school scams are documented by the FTC and the Education Department's inspector general Not confirmed Who sends messages under this name, and whether they are fake Fastest test Does it ask for money, a login or an ID number before you have checked it yourself? Where to report reportfraud.ftc.gov What the Education Connection scam message looks like
 How to judge any education message in two minutes
 Four questions decide most cases: who is asking, what they want, how fast, and how you can check it without using their contact details. A message that fails any one of them should not get a reply.
 Question Warning sign What to do 
 Who is asking? A vague name such as a connection, center, department or service, with no school or servicer you know Look up your school or servicer yourself and ask them if the message is theirs 
 What do they want? A fee for forgiveness, a refund or a grant; a login or ID number; a card number or gift cards Pay nothing and give nothing. Genuine help with federal loans does not require a fee 
 How fast? A deadline today, a limited time program, a threat to drop classes Stop. Real offices give you time and write to you through your account 
 How can you check? The only contact is the number or link in the message Find the number on your school's site or on your loan statement, not in the message 
 Does it know you? It recites a balance or account number to prove it is official That proves nothing; data about borrowers is traded 
 The order of actions after a message from Education Connection or any similar sender. What real student aid offices do, and what they do not
 The Education Department's federal student loan office is Federal Student Aid. A search of state consumer pages returned a notice from the District of Columbia's insurance and banking regulator saying that the Department does not run a body called a Student Loan Department, a name scammers like to use.
 The Education Department's inspector general publishes fraud alerts for students. Its 2026 alert, as we saw it in search results, warns that scammers ask for money in advance for things like a student aid refund, imitate the Education Department, the IRS or a school, use email addresses that nearly match real ones, and increasingly use AI generated voices.
 It advises checking that links lead to a .gov domain before you trust them. We read these points in search summaries and not in the full PDF, so read the alert itself before you rely on a detail.
 A line that comes up in consumer advice is that nothing a student loan debt relief company can do for you is something you cannot do yourself for free. Income driven repayment plans for federal loans are free to apply for through studentaid.gov.
 For private loans, the lender or servicer is the place to ask. If a message pushes you to pay a third party first, that is the opposite of how the free federal programs work.
 The FTC page lists the number of the Federal Student Aid Information Center as a way to check a claim, and the same page tells you to report scams at reportfraud.ftc.gov. We did not reach studentaid.gov during this check, so use the address you type yourself and not any link from a message.
 When the sender is not a thief but a lead seller
 Some education messages come from lead generators, companies that collect your details on a web form and pass them to schools. That is not the same as a scam, but it has produced real enforcement cases, so it deserves a separate explanation.
 In 2016 the FTC announced what was described as its first settlement with an education lead generator, Gigats, whose sites offered job listings that had no official link to the employers named.
 Warning: In 2019 Career Education Corp. agreed to pay 30 million dollars to settle FTC claims that it bought leads gathered by deceptive methods, including lead generators that posed as military recruiters, and that many resulting calls reached numbers on the Do Not Call Registry.
 We read these as press and law firm summaries in search results, not as the complaints.
 We mention them for one reason. If you once typed your phone number into a form promising scholarships, job help or free information, your number may have been passed to several schools and brokers, and the calls and texts that follow can come under many names.
 In that case the message is unwanted rather than criminal, and your control is to stop the sender and to refuse any form that sells your details to unnamed partners.
 None of this tells us which of these, if any, applies to a sender called Education Connection. We list it so that you can place your own message: a sender who knows you filled in a form is a lead seller, a sender who knows nothing real about you and demands money is a scammer.
 How to tell the Education Connection scam message is fake
 Do
 Contact your school or loan servicer through the number or address you already hold, never through a message. 
 Use studentaid.gov, typed by yourself, for any federal loan question. 
 Ask a relative or the school's financial aid office before you act on an offer that sounds too good. 
 Block and report unknown senders, and keep the carrier's spam filter on. 
 Use a different password for each account and turn on two step sign in. 
 Don't
 Pay a fee for loan forgiveness, a grant, a refund or repayment help. 
 Give a login, an ID number or a card number to someone who contacted you first. 
 Trust a caller because they know your balance or your school's name. 
 Act on a deadline in the message; the pressure is the tool. 
 Fill in web forms that promise free money for school and share your details with unnamed partners. 
 Is Education Connection scam dangerous? What the senders want
 What we checked for this guide, and what we could not
 This is a desk check. Our server made no request, because the subject is a name and not a web address, and we did not see any message. We read the FTC's page on student loan and education scams and searched for official warnings, enforcement cases and school notices that mention the name.
 Education Connection scam · desk check · 1 November 2026
 Plain request to an address Not made. The subject is a phrase, not a domain, and no address was given to us. 
 Malware address list No URLhaus entry exists for this name in the data our server reads on 1 November 2026. That says little about a scam text, which often uses links that change every day. 
 Regulator or school warning naming it None found in our searches of 1 November 2026. A search can miss a local notice, so this is not proof that no warning exists. 
 Who sends it Unknown. We could not see a message, a number, a sender address or a link. 
 Pattern fit The topic fits scam families the FTC describes: loan relief for a fee, callers who claim to act for the government or a school, and urgent payment demands. 
 Unconfirmed name, known scam pattern We have no proof that this name is a scam and no proof that it is safe. Judge the message by its demands. A fee, a deadline or a login request is enough reason to stop.
 What our desk check of 1 November 2026 could and could not confirm about the name. Why people search for it, and what the message usually looks like
 People usually search for a name like this right after an unexpected text, call or email. The message mentions their education, their loans or a school, and they cannot tell whether it is real. That doubt is correct: unsolicited education offers are one of the common ways scammers start a conversation.
 The FTC's page on student loan and education scams describes several versions. In the first, a caller or sender offers to lower your payments or get your loans forgiven, for a price. In the second, the caller says they are affiliated with Federal Student Aid or the Department of Education, which the FTC says they are not.
 In the third, someone poses as your school, says tuition is unpaid and threatens to drop your classes unless you send money right away. A fourth version rides on news about forgiveness and promises a new program that is open for a limited time.
 The FTC also notes that scammers may know things about your loan, such as the balance or an account number, and still be scammers. That detail makes a call feel official, but it proves little. Data about students and borrowers is bought, leaked and sold, and a caller who recites your balance may simply have read it from a list.
 Because we have not seen a message sent under this name, we cannot say which version, if any, it is. If yours matches one of these, treat it as the scam it resembles. If it matches none, the tests in the next section still apply.
 If you clicked the link or replied
 If you replied, paid or gave a login
 Act on what you gave, not on what you fear. Each kind of information has its own fix, and most of them take less than half an hour.
 1 You only read the message
 Nothing happened. Do not reply, do not tap links and do not call the number in it. Delete it, and block the number or address. On a phone you can also report a text by forwarding it to 7726 (SPAM), which most US carriers accept.
 2 You tapped a link but entered nothing
 Close the page. A link opened in the browser does not install anything by itself on a current phone or computer, but a page can ask you to install an app or a profile. If you did install something, remove it from your list of apps and run a scan with the built in Windows Security, Play Protect or your usual protection.
 3 You gave a password or an FSA ID
 Go to the real site by typing its address yourself and change the password. Do the same on every other site where you used that password. Turn on two step sign in. If the login was for studentaid.gov, check your account for changes to contact details or loan servicer.
 4 You paid by card, bank transfer or app
 Call your bank or card company at once, using the number on the card, and say you paid a scammer. Ask for a chargeback or a recall of the transfer. The faster you call, the better the chance. Keep the messages and receipts.
 5 You paid with gift cards or cryptocurrency
 Contact the card issuer or the exchange immediately. Recovery is much harder, but a prompt report can sometimes stop the money. File a report with the FTC regardless; it helps investigators connect cases.
 6 You gave your Social Security number or date of birth
 Consider freezing your credit with the three credit bureaus, which is free in the US, and check your credit reports for accounts you did not open.
 If you run the organisation whose name is being used
 If your school, college or company calls itself some kind of connection or center and students report fake messages in your name, say so publicly and give people one safe way to verify you.
 Publish a short notice on your site that lists the only numbers, email domains and web addresses you use, and says what you never ask for by text or phone, such as payment by gift card or a login.
 Tell your registrar and your email provider if a lookalike domain appears, and report the lookalike to the FTC. Staff who answer student calls should be able to confirm in one sentence whether a message came from you.
 If your own website was hacked and is being used to send or host these messages, change all administrator passwords, update the site software and plugins, and check for files you did not add. We cannot tell from the facts we have whether any such case exists here.
 What is still unknown
 We do not know who sends messages under the name Education Connection, how many people have received them, whether the messages are fraud or unwanted marketing, or whether a single operation stands behind them. We made no site test and saw no message.
 This page will be refreshed if reported addresses appear in the malware reports we read or if a regulator or school names the sender. Until then, treat the name as unproven either way, and let the content of each message decide what you do. If you have a message, a screenshot or a web address, report it to the FTC so the picture becomes clearer for everyone.
 What to do after the Education Connection scam e-mail
 If you only received the message and clicked nothing, step 3 is all you need.
 If you clicked the link or typed anything on the page it opened, do every step, starting with the password.
 1 Step 1 : Change the password you typed on the fake page
 If you typed a password on the page the Education Connection scam message opened, assume the sender has it. Go to the real site by typing its address yourself and change the password there, choosing one you have never used.
 Change it anywhere else the same password was used, and sign out all other sessions if the service offers it. Any browser on Windows 11 or Windows 10 will do, as long as you do not follow the e-mail's link.
 Microsoft account, Security page (account.microsoft.com/security): Change password. Full procedure with screenshots: Turn on two-step verification / secure a hacked account 
 Get a free scan and check if your PC is infected.
 Fortect scans Windows for malware and the damage it leaves behind. It does not decrypt files.
 Remove it now To use the full-featured product, you have to purchase a license for Fortect. The scan is free. 2 Step 2 : Turn on two-step verification
 With two-step verification on, a stolen password alone no longer opens the account, because a sign-in from a new device also needs a code from your phone.
 Switch it on for the e-mail account first, then for banking, shopping and social accounts that use that address.
 Check the recovery phone, the recovery e-mail and any forwarding rules while you are in the settings, since attackers change them to come back. The pages are the same on Windows 11 and Windows 10.
 Microsoft account: Manage how I sign in, where two-step verification and the sign-in methods are. Full procedure with screenshots: Turn on two-step verification / secure a hacked account 
 3 Step 3 : Report the e-mail and delete it
 Do not reply and do not click anything else in the message. In Outlook select the e-mail and choose Report > Report phishing ; in Gmail open the three-dot menu next to Reply and pick Report phishing .
 That trains the filter for everyone on the service, and the message goes to the junk folder. If the e-mail came to a work address, forward it to your IT team as an attachment first.
 The steps are the same in the web mail and the mail apps on Windows 11 and Windows 10.
 New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the web: Report > Report phishing. Full procedure with screenshots: Report a phishing e-mail 
 4 Step 4 : Scan the PC if you opened a file from the message
 A fake sign-in page only steals what you type, so most readers can skip this step. If the Education Connection scam e-mail made you download or open a file, delete it and scan the PC.
 In Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Scan options , run a Full scan and then Microsoft Defender Antivirus (offline scan) > Scan now . The offline scan restarts Windows 11 or Windows 10 and takes about 15 minutes.
 Windows 11: Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Scan options. Full procedure with screenshots: Run a Microsoft Defender Offline scan 
 Did the manual steps not help?
 Get a free scan and check if your PC is infected. Fortect scans Windows for malware, unwanted programs and the Windows damage they leave behind.
 Remove it now To use the full-featured product, you have to purchase a license for Fortect. The scan is free. How to report Education Connection scam
 How to report it, and why it is worth the time
 Report the message at reportfraud.ftc.gov. The FTC page on student loan and education scams names that address, and a report gives investigators the sender, the number and the wording they use to link cases.
 A good report includes the date and time, how the message arrived, the phone number or email address it came from, the exact name the sender used, any web address in it (copy it, do not open it), what they asked for, and whether you paid. Take a screenshot before you delete the message. If you are outside the United States, use your national consumer or cybercrime reporting service instead.
 Also tell your school or loan servicer. They may be able to warn other students, and a school can often say at once whether it ever uses a given name. If the message pretended to be from your school, the school's real office can confirm that it did not send it.

 Report the message at reportfraud.ftc.gov. The FTC page on student loan and education scams names that address, and a report gives investigators the sender, the number and the wording they use to link cases.
 A good report includes the date and time, how the message arrived, the phone number or email address it came from, the exact name the sender used, any web address in it (copy it, do not open it), what they asked for, and whether you paid. Take a screenshot before you delete the message. If you are outside the United States, use your national consumer or cybercrime reporting service instead.
 Also tell your school or loan servicer. They may be able to warn other students, and a school can often say at once whether it ever uses a given name. If the message pretended to be from your school, the school's real office can confirm that it did not send it.
 Questions about Education Connection scam
 Is Education Connection a scam?
 We cannot confirm it. We found no regulator, school or security company warning that names a sender called Education Connection, so we do not call the name a scam, and we do not call it safe.
 Student loan and school scams are real and well documented, and vague education names are a common cover. Judge your message by its demands: a fee, a deadline or a request for a login is enough reason to stop and verify through your school or loan servicer yourself.
 I got a text from Education Connection. What should I do?
 Do not tap the link, do not reply and do not call the number in the text. Check the claim by contacting your school or your loan servicer through a number you already have.
 If the text asks for money, a password or an ID number, treat it as a scam. You can forward the text to 7726 (SPAM), block the number, and report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Take a screenshot first so that you keep the details.
 Is an Education Connection phone call legitimate?
 We cannot tell from the name alone. A genuine school or servicer will not mind if you hang up and call back on a number from your own records.
 The FTC says callers who claim to be affiliated with Federal Student Aid or the Department of Education are not, and that scammers may know your balance or account number. Do not give a login, an ID or a card number to a caller who contacted you first, and do not pay a fee for relief.
 Can Education Connection get my student loans forgiven?
 Be careful with any sender who promises it. The FTC describes scammers who offer to lower payments or get loans forgiven for a price.
 Programs for federal loans, such as income driven repayment, are free to apply for through studentaid.gov, and consumer advice repeats that a debt relief company cannot do anything you cannot do yourself for free. For private loans, ask the lender. Pay no one before you have checked the offer with the official source.
 What if I already gave my details or paid?
 Act on what you gave. For a card or bank payment, call your bank using the number on the card and ask for a chargeback or recall. For a password or FSA ID, change it on the real site and everywhere you reused it, and turn on two step sign in.
 For gift cards or cryptocurrency, contact the issuer or exchange at once. For a Social Security number, consider a free credit freeze. Then report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
 Is it a virus, and do I need to remove something from my phone or computer?
 A message by itself is not a virus, and there is nothing called Education Connection to uninstall. A risk appears only if you installed an app, opened a file or entered a password on a linked page.
 In that case remove any app you did not choose, run a scan with Windows Security or Play Protect, and change the passwords you typed. If you only read the message, delete it and block the sender.
 Could Education Connection be a genuine company that sells leads?
 It could, and we cannot rule it out. Education lead generators collect details on web forms and pass them to schools, and the FTC has taken action against some of them, for example Gigats in 2016 and, in 2019, a 30 million dollar settlement with Career Education Corp. over purchased leads.
 If you remember filling in a form, the contact may be marketing. You can still demand that the sender stop, and refuse any fee or login request.
 How do I check if a message really comes from my school or the Department of Education?
 Do not use the contact details in the message. Find your school's number on its own website or your loan servicer's number on a statement, and ask whether it sent the message. For federal loans, sign in at studentaid.gov by typing the address yourself.
 The Education Department's inspector general advises checking that links lead to a .gov domain, and notes that fraudsters use email addresses that nearly match real ones, so read the sender address letter by letter.
 Where do I report an education scam?
 Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Include the date, the sender's number or email address, the name used, any web address (copied, not opened), what was asked for and whether you paid.
 Also tell your school or loan servicer, and your bank if you paid. Outside the United States, use your national consumer or cybercrime reporting service. Reports help investigators connect cases that look separate to each victim.
 Will Fortect remove Education Connection scam?
 Fortect scans Windows for malware and unwanted programs and repairs the system files and settings they change, and its free scan shows what it finds on your PC before you decide anything. 
 For Education Connection scam, follow the plan above as well: the browser steps take back permissions and settings that no scanner treats as a threat, and uninstalling the program that brought it removes the source.
 Run Microsoft Defender's full scan and, if anything was found, its offline scan as a second opinion. If the symptoms are gone after the plan and both scans are clean, there is nothing more to do.
